Its largest cliques have three nodes; A, B, C is drawn in the accent color and B, C, D ties it. The card gives the treewidth as the largest clique size minus one, 3 − 1 = 2." width="100%"} The treewidth measures how tree-like a graph is (see `tree_decomposition()`). It is NP-hard to compute in general, but for a chordal graph it is simply the size of the largest clique minus one, found in linear time. Use it to gauge the cost of inference on a triangulated graphical model or of dynamic programming over a clique tree. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The treewidth (`-1` for an empty graph). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed or not chordal. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The maximal cliques of `chordal_graph_cliques()` are exactly the bags of an optimal tree decomposition, so the width is the largest clique size minus one. Matches NetworkX's `chordal_graph_treewidth`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#8b01644c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E")]) g.chordal_graph_treewidth() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: :::
